title: Bad Trips Guide, Round 28
intro: Round 28 (2026-11-09). Your round 27 is in: both sentences of your post are back, your first five minutes is one piece again with the panic loop and your story of the voice, and your aftermath list is in as you wrote it. The helper's Don't heading and its two paragraphs went, since your first five minutes says them now. I kept the practice paragraph ("If a practice like meditation or fasting brought this on, ...") right after your reminder, since it's that reminder's practice case. Typos fixed: "chanting, on them", "aftewards", "for benefit all involved" (to "to benefit all involved"), "onr", and the shame guide's link, which needed its http:// to open.

You asked for my best first, then options with pros and cons, and the choices that matter most. The first card is what I could fix: three terms in your aftermath list explained where they're used. The other five are the choices, most impactful first: how your method gets into the parts people use in trouble, the Fear/Panic Loop now that your first five minutes has it, how much of the aftermath list the guide needs, what For the Person Helping is now for, and one safety point, Syrian rue, to settle before the guide goes live. Each says what I'd pick and why.

edits.before: Anxiety and fear: with this pattern, it helps to first figure out what is providing the stimulation for the anxiety. CBT-style reality testing is one way to do that which could be explored with a therapist if it persists, but can be done without one to start with. In general, it can help to have grounding/relaxing routines (like morning or bedtime yin yoga, meeting a friend for lunch).

suggestions.title: 1. Your method in the parts people use in trouble: how?
suggestions.question:
A fresh reader found 15 places where the guide gives generic advice where your method would change what the reader or helper does ([where](https://github.com/u-dont-existDOTcom/joel-articles/blob/claude/bad-trips-20261105/articles/bad-trips/humanize/h37-20261108/beliefs/GENERIC.md)). Your first five minutes, your don'ts and your aftermath list now carry it, which leaves 10: the sitter's script, Alone at 3 a.m., the helper's Do list, the Grounding Menu's hand on the heart and breath line, the thinking traps, Give the Session's preparation, Abuse Memories' step after sleep, Shadow Thoughts' in-trip move, and the questions after the aftermath list.

A (my pick): I move or quote sentences the guide already has, where it gives your method, into those places, one approve card each, starting with the four that matter most: Alone at 3 a.m. (someone with no sitter: "Can I send love to the one who's suffering?" and the hand on the heart), the breath line ("I can love the part of me that feels it."), Give the Session's preparation ("So train before you need it, sending love to a frightening image ...") and the thinking traps ("young parts of you that are still waiting for love ..."). Pro: your method where it's used, in sentences the guide already has, quick for you to approve. Con: a moved sentence can need a joining word, and the places read AI now, so they may still need your hand for Pangram.

B: teaching cards, one or two places at a time, for you to write each with your method in it. Pro: your voice and your view, and they read Human. Con: your time, ten places.

C: leave them. Pro: no work. Con: the guide stays generic where it's used.
suggestions.why: This is the change that matters most to what the guide is: your method, not generic trip-sitting advice, at the moment someone needs it.
suggestions.stays: Whichever you pick, nothing is written for you: only sentences the guide already has, moved, or your own versions.
suggestions.advice_note: A, then B for any place where a moved sentence doesn't fit.

suggestions.question:
A (my pick): keep all eight kinds as your version has them, with the three terms on the first card and the Syrian rue question settled. Pro: each kind now says what to do and why, with your remedies, and it read High as you wrote it. Con: it's long (about 520 words), and two kinds, visual distortions and paranoia, are medical enough that the reader also needs the call-for-help lists at the top.

B: keep the five kinds a reader can recognize in themselves (anxiety and fear, sleep, shame, existential shock, bodily restlessness) and move visual distortions, derealization and paranoia to "Bring in mental-health support when:", each with your remedy in a line. Pro: shorter, and the three that may need a professional sit with the call-for-help lines. Con: it splits your version, and those remedies move away from the days-after list where the reader looks.

C: cut the list to its first paragraph and point to the sections that cover each kind. Pro: shortest. Con: loses your remedies and the days-after view.

suggestions.title: 5. Syrian rue in your paranoia line: a safety point
suggestions.question:
Your paranoia line names "the relatively safe and natural antipsychotics mentioned in this guide, like DMSO, syrian rue OIL, and niacin". The guide doesn't mention Syrian rue anywhere else, and its serotonin syndrome section lists "harmala/ayahuasca-type MAOI exposure" among the things to stop. Syrian rue (Peganum harmala) is the classic harmala source: its seed extracts strongly inhibit MAO-A, mainly through harmaline and harmine, and that inhibition is the main cause of its toxic effects ([a review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3841998/)). Someone with lingering paranoia may still be on an antidepressant or an MDMA-type drug, the combination the guide warns about.

A (my pick): say what "syrian rue OIL" is (if it's an oil used on the skin or by smell, as your capitals suggest, say so), and add the harmala warning where it's named: not with antidepressants, MDMA, other MAOIs or the rest of the serotonin list. Pro: keeps your remedy with what a reader needs to use it safely. Con: a few more words in your line.

B: take Syrian rue out of the line until it has its own place in the guide, with its warning. Pro: the safest wording now. Con: your remedy goes for now.

C: keep the line as it is. Con: it names a remedy the guide never explains, next to a warning against it.

Also, in the bodily-restlessness line, "my trusty relaxing herbs and natural antipsychotics listed above": no herbs are listed above it. Name them, or point to "Mental Stabilizers That Don't Abort the Trip".
suggestions.why: It's the one place in your new lines where a reader could get hurt following the guide as written.
suggestions.stays: Everything else in the line, whichever you pick.
suggestions.advice_note: A, or B if the oil isn't different from the seeds.
